title: Becoming Muslim
hookLine: a person becomes Muslim by sincerely saying the shahada, often before witnesses

lines: THE WORDS, A PHRASE AT A TIME.
cards: The Friday prayer is over, and nobody is leaving yet. A woman stands near the front, a little pale, holding a folded card she doesn't end up needing.
The imam says the words a phrase at a time, and she repeats them after him. Ashhadu an la ilaha illallah. Wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah.
Then the room says Allahu akbar, and a line forms of people who have never met her, waiting to hug her or shake her hand. That's one way it happens. What actually made her Muslim was invisible.

teach.b: Year one met people new to Islam; today, the moment itself. A person becomes Muslim by saying the two sentences of the shahadah and meaning them. No course to pass first, no fee.
First, it has to be free.
The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "There is no compulsion in religion." A testimony forced out of someone isn't a testimony. Second, sincerity lives where no one can check it.
Sahih Muslim records a hard story. In a battle, a companion named Usama overtook an enemy fighter, who said la ilaha illallah. Usama struck him anyway, thinking he only said it out of fear.

teach.h: DID YOU SPLIT OPEN HIS HEART?
teach.b: When the Prophet heard, he asked him, and kept asking: did you split open his heart, to know whether it said it or not? People hear the words; only God sees the heart.
So the community takes the words at face value and leaves the rest to God. Third, the witnesses.
The shahadah is often said in front of others, at a mosque or with friends, sometimes with a certificate afterward for practical needs. The witnesses can't see the heart either.
What they can do is know, and welcome: show up, teach the prayer, invite someone to iftar in Ramadan. Fourth, a beginning, not a finish line.
The person who says it on Friday will still need to learn how to pray on Saturday. Some teachers point here to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari: actions are judged by intentions.
The intention comes first, the learning follows, and nobody expects a new Muslim to know it all on day one.

how: A person becomes Muslim by sincerely saying the shahadah, often at a mosque before witnesses, after which the community usually greets them and helps them learn the prayer and the basics of practice.

o: finishing a course of study and passing a test
being accepted after an imam checks your heart
saying the two sentences freely, and meaning them

p: did you split open his heart?

s: a person must finish a long course before saying the shahadah
the testimony, said freely and meant, is what makes a person Muslim; the learning follows.
the Qur'an says there is no compulsion in religion
the witnesses decide whether the shahadah was sincere
only God sees the heart; the community takes the words at face value.

games.q: you are Usama. in the fighting, the man in front of you suddenly says la ilaha illallah. you're sure he only said it out of fear. what does the Prophet later say?
o: you were right to judge his motive.
did you split open his heart to know?
words spoken in battle don't count.
games.why: Sahih Muslim records his rebuke: people hear the words, and only God sees the heart.

practice: Think of a time you were new somewhere, and who made it easier: a name remembered, a seat saved, a question answered without a sigh.

Now bring to mind someone who is new right now, perhaps someone who has recently become Muslim, perhaps a newcomer of any kind, and picture one small welcome you could give them. If you pray, you can ask good for them.

wordCard.voice: Becoming Muslim. Two sentences, said freely and meant, with the heart left to God and the welcome left to the community. Today's word.

orig.note: he became Muslim, he surrendered himself; the same root as إِسْلَام (is-LAAM).

carryVoice: Your line: said sincerely. The heart is left to God, and the welcome to everyone else. Next: what the testimony asks.

sources.q: There is no compulsion in religion.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 96 (Usama ibn Zayd: did you split open his heart?)
